newsitem.title: HAITI: Aristide launches new Haitian political group.
newsitem.headline: Aristide launches new Haitian political group.

text.p: Former priest and president Jean-Bertrand Aristide on Sunday created a new pulpit for his political message to the poor of Haiti at the official launch of a new political organisation.

Addressing some 1,500 supporters in the southern city of Jacmel, Aristide was careful to stress that the formation of the group did not signal a break with the Lavalas coalition that brought him to power in 1990.
"People are asking whether this means we are angry with anyone, and I say 'no, just the opposite,'" said Aristide.

However below where Aristide stood was a sign that read "We don't want those false Lavalas," highlighting ongoing rumours that Aristide sought to distance himself from the current Lavalas administration.
The creation of the group, called the Assembly of the Lavalas Family, was Aristide's first step back into politics since he ended his presidential term in February, replaced by President Rene Preval.
Aristide came to power in a landslide election, riding a wave of popular support from those who heard his fiery sermons to some of Haiti's poorest.
He was ousted in a military coup that lasted three years and left some 5,000 Haitians dead before Aristide was returned in 1994 by U.S. troops.
While both Preval and Aristide, who were once called twins for their similar political views, insisted they were still good friends, their positions on key issues drifted apart.
Aristide has spoken out against the privatisation of some government businesses, a move championed by Preval.
The new organisation, which will have representatives in Haiti's 10 departments, will run candidates in upcoming senatorial elections and other future elections, according to an aide to Aristide.
Aristide supporters said they hoped the organisation would give them a stronger voice in Haitian politics.
"They must listen to us," yelled one woman waving photos of Aristide in the crowd during his speech.

Some observers noted the photos of Aristide handed out during the rally gave the meeting the feel of a campaign, raising questions about whether the organisation will eventually be his springboard in the 2000 elections.
The former president has refused to comment on whether he will run in the 2000 elections.
